subject: Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?

messages.author: 7d0849fb70633078
messages.subject: Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
parts:
Hi Stan Team,

I'm a big fan of Stan and Gelman's Bayesian Data Analysis. I really enjoyed Bob Carpenter's and Michael Betancourt's youtube videos. In the RMHMC video I was blown away by how far the maximum likelihood point of the funnel was from where all the mass of the funnel was. It scared me away from point estimates which are all too common in the Systems Biology literature.

Anyway my colleague and I have a system of ODEs that we're using to describe some longitudinal mRNA data. So far my colleague said he's been using particle swarm optimization to find a maximum likelihood estimate. He gets about 200 ML estimates (which are all different by the way because our parameter space is non-convex), he throws out about 50 of the estimates that "don't give qualitatively correct results". On the remaining 150 estimates he takes quantiles to get estimates of the parameters and confidence bounds around those estimates in what turns out to be a very ad-hoc and probably quite misleading Bayesian analysis.

To me the problem is begging us to run HMC to get actual draws from the posterior. These parameters represent knowledge of a human being's blood clotting system so it's actually very elucidating to see what the most probable values are. The problem is that our system is stiff and as I understand Stan does not support non-stiff ODEs as of now. I figure if you're using something like Newton''s method, calculating the gradient of the objective function (which involves finding the change in the solution at every time point) won't be too bad, especially with autodiff. I'm guessing with more fancy Runge-Kutta methods the problem starts to get really sticky. Where is Stan at in terms of supporting non-stiff ODEs?

Also, our problem is definitely multi-modal, but I am hoping that once RMHMC comes out for Stan that won't be so big of a problem. Am I naive in thinking that? When do you all anticipate RMHMC coming out?

Thanks,
Arya

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
parts:
CVODE was implemented internally in Stan 2.9, but has only been exposed in
the CmdStan interface.  So if you want to get started you try it there.  We’re
looking at CVODES and other solvers, as well, but that’s still in development.
It would be cool to see if you can get any traction in fitting your model in 
CmdStan already.

A prototype of RHMC might be added to the internal code soon (whenever I
get around to it) but it will be limited in its application.  The problem is that
RHMC requires second and third-order derivatives but we haven’t really
tested our higher-order autodiff all that well.  In particular, it’s unlikely that
the higher-order autodiff will play well with the ODE solvers.

In any case, RHMC won’t help too much with multi modality.  For that you’d
need _Adiabatic Monte Carlo_, but that’s still a research project.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
parts:
I certainly wouldn't trust the analysis you described, because
the computation has no interpretation (you can't just find different
modes and call that variance).

We have a non-stiff ODE solver in all the Stan interfaces,
and a stiff ODE solver in CmdStan 2.9 (and it should be in the
2.10 release of RStan).

Nobody has a solution for combinatorial multimodality. The
ability of a single chain to mix will through very limited multimodality
will depend on the trough between the modes and how easy it is to pass
through. And there are some techniques that'll help there, but none
that are implemented in Stan.

I'm curious what the longitudinal study of mRNA is. I just
started to do some work on isoform (splice variant) expression.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
parts:
The documentation is still incomplete, but when you use CmdStan 2.9
the CVODE library should automatically build and link.  Then you just
need to use the “integrate_ode_cvode” function.  It takes the same
arguments at “integrate_ode” except there are three additional
arguments: absolute and relative tolerances and maximum number
of steps.  I’d recommend starting with 1e-10, 1e-10, 1e6 and playing
around from there.

What causes the multi modality in the model?

Just read the first bit of your Adiabatic Monte Carlo paper. That is some really cool stuff! I wish there was more people working on full posterior inference in computer science. Any idea why the machine learning conferences focus more on maximum likelihood or variational methods? My department is hiring a machine learning professor this year and that's the impression I've been getting during the talks.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Update on Stiff ODEs and RMHMC?
parts: Thanks! The states could increase and decrease due to multiple other states. So a species Z could increase because it's really sensitive to X being high, or alternatively it could increase not because X is high but because a third species Y is high.

I’m not sure how that manifests as multi modality.  You could certainly have strong
correlations and potentially partial non-identifiabilities, which HMC can tackle, but
I don’t see how that leads to separate modes.  Typically separates modes requires
a mixture hiding somewhere.

Just read the first bit of your Adiabatic Monte Carlo paper. That is some really cool stuff! I wish there was more people working on full posterior inference in computer science. Any idea why the machine learning conferences focus more on maximum likelihood or variational methods? My department is hiring a machine learning professor this year and that's the impression I've been getting during the talks.

It’s best not to get me ranting.  Needless to say, I do not advocate trusting computer
scientists or the typical machine learner to a robust statistical analysis, _especially_
in science.
